profile.headline: Software Engineer at Google working on making Chrome more usable and secure for every user
profile.summary:
I'm a software engineer on the Google Chrome security team working on network security and security UX.

I completed my PhD at UC Berkeley advised by Prof. David Wagner. My dissertation studied the quantitative effects of modern peer code review on software security. Before that, I worked on usable security, Internet routing security, anti-censorship systems, and privacy-preserving cryptographic systems.

positions.title: Graduate Student Researcher
positions.description:
- Designed and ran large-scale measurements and experiments on the relationships between software development process and software security and quality.
- Built novel state of the art quantification models using TensorFlow and text-classification techniques to allow large-scale analysis of software issues.
- Created a novel privilege-separation architecture to improve privacy of rich video applications.
- Developed extensions to the Android operating system to attribute resource usage by apps, and performed user studies to show they were significantly more effective at informing users of resource usage than stock Android.
- Discovered and reported multiple previously unknown security vulnerabilities in T-Mobile Wi-Fi Calling and Android next-generation IMS cellular authentication, and worked with T-Mobile to fix these vulnerabilities.
- Surveyed iOS developers and users about resource usage strings, and found that usage strings are effective at making users more comfortable about resource requests, but developers are poorly informed about them.

positions.title: Software Engineer Intern
positions.description:
Worked with the Chrome Security team. My main project was designing and implementing an experience sampling platform for Chrome (consisting of a new extension API, instrumenting various security UI surfaces to trigger API events, a custom App Engine backend to handle survey responses, and a Chrome extension to handle experience sampling events and serve surveys to participants).

I also helped improve various security UI problems in Chrome, such as the extension permissions prompt, and the plugin blocking UI.

positions.title: Undergraduate Research Assistant
positions.description:
- Performed critical security analysis of new "decoy routing" anti-censorship systems, applying prior experience with network security and Internet routing to demonstrate potential attacks by state-level adversaries.
- Designed, analyzed, and implemented privacy-preserving primitives for uniform random sampling, using specialized cryptosystems to achieve novel privacy properties.
- Developed virtualized software router testbed for studying the behavior of Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) routers.

positions.title: Lead Web Developer
positions.description: Led development of new websites and systems for a small web design and social media consulting firm, primarily using the LAMP platform and the WordPress CMS system. Advised the selection of new technologies and solutions for clients and other ventures, as well as the development of new work-flow processes. Assisted in supervising and advising two other developers.

positions.title: Research Intern
positions.description: Supported by an NSF Research Experience for Undergraduates (REU) grant. Worked with Prof. Nikita Borisov on Protecting Email from Curious Observers with Provider Encrypt on Receipt.

company.name: Information Trust Institute, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

projects.title: Routing Around Decoys
projects.description: A new direction of anti-censorship systems called "decoy routing" redirect traffic in an "end-to-middle" fashion instead of the traditional "end-to-end" proxy design that systems like Tor use. Our work extended the threat model to include routing adversaries---those that could change or influence routing policy in the network---and showed that such adversaries could fundamentally break the security of decoy routing systems, making them much harder to deploy.

projects.title: Randomness Exposed – An Attack on Hosted Virtual Machines
projects.description: Attempted to cryptographically break the Linux pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) of a guest OS running on QEMU-KVM by using the host to monitor the entropy input to the guest’s PRNG. We failed to achieve a cryptographic break, but we were able to reduce the complexity of predicting pseudo-random numbers generated by the guest OS.

publications.publisher: ACM Workshop on Security and Privacy in Smartphones and Mobile Devices (SPSM '16) · Oct 1, 2016

publications.title: The effect of developer-specified explanations for permission requests on smartphone user behavior
publications.publisher: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '14) · Jan 1, 2014
